questions.q: How is a drawdown value at a given point in time calculated?
options: The return on that single day, expressed as a percentage
The current equity value's percentage distance below the running maximum (high-water mark) reached so far
The average of all negative daily returns up to that point
The difference between today's equity and yesterday's equity
questions.explain: Drawdown = equity / running_max - 1, where running_max is the highest equity value reached up to that point (the high-water mark). It answers how far below the best prior point you currently are.

questions.q: Why might risk managers and allocators ask about maximum drawdown before, or in addition to, the Sharpe ratio?
options: Maximum drawdown is easier to calculate than Sharpe
Maximum drawdown answers directly how much could realistically have been lost at the worst possible moment, which Sharpe doesn't capture on its own
Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown are always mathematically identical
Maximum drawdown is required by law for all strategy reports
questions.explain: Max drawdown directly answers 'what's the worst loss I could have experienced holding this strategy at the worst time to have started,' which is a different and often more viscerally important question than a volatility-normalized average return.

questions.q: Two strategies both have a 12% maximum drawdown. Why might they still be very different to actually hold?
options: They can't actually be different if the max drawdown is the same
One could recover from its drawdown in three weeks while the other takes eight months — recovery time is a separate dimension from drawdown depth
Maximum drawdown already accounts for recovery time
The difference would only matter for strategies trading different asset classes
questions.explain: Maximum drawdown only measures depth, not duration. Recovery time (how long until equity reaches a new high after the trough) is a separate, equally important measure of how painful a drawdown actually is to live through.

questions.q: What does the "longest underwater streak" measure, and how does it differ from maximum drawdown?
options: It is identical to maximum drawdown, just expressed in days instead of percent
It measures the longest consecutive run of days spent below any prior equity peak, capturing prolonged grinding pain even without a single dramatic new low
It measures how many separate drawdowns occurred over the whole period
It can only be computed if the strategy never recovers
questions.explain: The longest underwater streak counts consecutive days where drawdown is negative, regardless of how deep it gets at any single point — capturing a different kind of pain (prolonged time without a new high) than the single worst drawdown value.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that a backtested maximum drawdown should be treated as a floor rather than a ceiling for what to expect live?
options: Because backtested drawdowns are always exactly half of live drawdowns
Because the biases covered in Chapter 4 (look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, underestimated costs) tend to flatter a backtest, meaning live drawdowns are often worse, not better
Because live markets never have drawdowns, only backtests do
Because drawdown cannot be measured in a live account at all
questions.explain: Since the common backtesting biases tend to make backtests look better than real trading would have been, a backtested max drawdown is typically an understatement of what a live drawdown could realistically look like — a floor, not a worst-case ceiling.
